overview.text: The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped endocrine gland at the front of the neck. It releases thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), hormones that regulate how the body uses energy and affect nearly every organ. The pituitary gland helps control thyroid hormone production by releasing TSH, which signals the thyroid how much T3 and T4 to make. The thyroid’s C cells also produce calcitonin, which helps lower blood calcium and counteracts parathyroid hormone. Together, these functions make the thyroid important to energy use and a contributor to calcium balance. Too much or too little thyroid hormone is associated with hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.

key_facts.text: The thyroid sits at the front of the neck and is commonly described as butterfly-shaped.
T4 is thyroxine; T3 is triiodothyronine. The hormones help regulate the body’s use of energy.
TSH is made by the pituitary gland and signals the thyroid how much T3 and T4 to produce.
Thyroid C cells make calcitonin, which helps lower blood calcium and opposes parathyroid hormone’s action.
Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid makes more hormone than the body needs; hypothyroidism means it does not make enough.
